subject: Civil Engineering
title: The Brooklyn Bridge
description: A quick, practical guide to The Brooklyn Bridge.

hook.text: In 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the longest suspension bridge ever built — by far.

buildup.text: John Roebling designed it, but died before construction began. His son took over.

discovery.text: Workers in caissons 78 feet underwater suffered decompression sickness — the bends.

twist.text: Washington Roebling became paralyzed from the bends and directed work by telescope.

climax.text: It took 14 years. On opening day, 150,000 people walked across in celebration.

punchline.text: A bridge built by a family who sacrificed everything for it.

quiz.question: What debilitating condition affected Brooklyn Bridge workers?
options: Lead poisoning from the paint used on the cables
Decompression sickness from working in pressurized caissons underwater
Heat stroke from working in direct sunlight on the towers

details.summary: The Brooklyn Bridge, completed in 1883, was the first suspension bridge to use steel wire cables and the longest suspension span in the world at 486 meters.
details.whyItMatters: The Brooklyn Bridge pioneered steel cable technology, pneumatic caisson foundations, and suspension bridge construction methods used in every major suspension bridge that followed.
takeaways: It was the first suspension bridge to use steel wire cables instead of iron
Pneumatic caissons sunk to bedrock caused decompression sickness in workers
The Roeblings' family sacrifice became a legendary engineering story

faq.question: What is caisson disease and how did it affect Brooklyn Bridge workers?
faq.answer: Caisson disease, now called decompression sickness or the bends, occurs when workers in compressed air environments return to normal pressure too quickly. Dissolved nitrogen forms bubbles in the blood, causing severe pain, paralysis, or death. Washington Roebling was permanently disabled by it.

faq.question: Why was using steel wire instead of iron wire so important?
faq.answer: Steel wire has roughly twice the tensile strength of iron wire, meaning cables could be smaller and lighter while supporting greater loads. This advance made longer suspension spans practical and more economical. Every subsequent suspension bridge adopted steel wire cables.
